blocks.content: RDBMS versus NoSQL compared two broad categories of database from the outside. Database Architecture goes one level deeper, looking at how a database is actually built internally, the real layers a query passes through between the moment you type it and the moment rows actually come back.

Understanding this internal structure is not just academic curiosity. It genuinely explains why some queries are fast and others are slow, why a crash does not necessarily lose your data, and why the planner sometimes makes choices that surprise you. This topic walks through that internal stack layer by layer.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032368870-281774111.png
blocks.alt: Database architecture looks at how a database is actually built internally, beneath the SQL you type

blocks.content: 1. The Layer Stack

A query genuinely passes through several distinct layers before it returns any actual data. Your query, sent from the application, first reaches the query parser and planner, which checks it and decides how to actually execute it. That plan is handed to the execution engine, which carries it out.

The execution engine reads through the buffer pool, an in memory cache of disk pages, before ever touching the actual storage engine on disk. Each of these layers exists for a genuine reason, and understanding what each one actually does explains a great deal about real database behavior.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032370967-365030805.png
blocks.alt: A query passes through the parser and planner, the execution engine, the buffer pool, and finally the storage engine on disk

blocks.content: 2. What the Parser and Planner Actually Do
blocks.text: 2. What the Parser and Planner Actually Do

blocks.content: The parser first checks that your query is syntactically valid SQL, catching a missing comma or a misspelled keyword before any real work begins. Once the query is valid, the planner decides the actual order of operations needed to execute it, which table to read first, whether to use an available index, how to join multiple tables together.

The planner produces an execution plan, a concrete, ordered set of steps the execution engine will actually follow. Two queries that look similar on the surface can produce very different plans, depending on the data, the available indexes, and the database own internal statistics about the table.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032372639-188813346.png
blocks.alt: The parser and planner check syntax validity, decide the actual order of operations, and produce a concrete execution plan for the engine to follow

3. Why the Buffer Pool Matters So Much
blocks.text: 3. Why the Buffer Pool Matters So Much

blocks.content: Reading directly from disk every single time a query runs is genuinely slow, disk access is orders of magnitude slower than reading from memory, even with fast modern storage. If every query had to hit disk directly, database performance would be dramatically worse than what you actually experience day to day.

Keeping frequently used pages cached in the buffer pool means most real reads in a healthy, well used database actually hit memory, not disk, which is genuinely fast. This is a large part of why a database that has been running and handling queries for a while often feels noticeably faster than one that was just restarted, with a cold, empty buffer pool.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032374153-592655418.png
blocks.alt: Reading directly from disk every time is genuinely slow; keeping frequently used pages cached in the buffer pool means most real reads hit fast memory instead

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Assuming a database always reads directly from disk on every query. In practice, a healthy database serves the large majority of real reads from its in memory buffer pool, not from disk directly.
4. What the Storage Engine Actually Manages
blocks.text: 4. What the Storage Engine Actually Manages

blocks.content: The storage engine manages how rows are physically laid out on disk, the actual bytes and pages that represent your table data. It also manages how indexes are physically structured, the separate data structures that let the database find specific rows quickly without scanning an entire table.

And critically, the storage engine manages how writes are made durable, ensuring that once a write is acknowledged as successful, it genuinely survives a crash, a power failure, or an unexpected restart, rather than silently disappearing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032375701-440455895.png
blocks.alt: The storage engine manages physical row layout, physical index structure, and how writes are made durable even after a crash

blocks.content: 5. A Worked Query Through the Stack
blocks.text: 5. A Worked Query Through the Stack

blocks.content: Tracing a simple query through this entire stack makes the layers concrete. A simple select with a where clause first reaches the planner, which decides whether to use an available index on the filtered column, or fall back to scanning the entire table if no useful index exists.

The execution engine then fetches the matching pages, checking the buffer pool first before ever going to disk. Once the matching rows are found, they are returned to your application, having passed through every one of these layers along the way.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032377218-211524346.png
blocks.alt: A worked query: the planner decides whether to use an index, the engine fetches matching pages checking the buffer pool first, then returns the matching rows

blocks.content: 6. The Write Ahead Log

Most real databases use a write ahead log to guarantee durability without waiting for every write to be fully applied to its final location on disk. When a write request arrives, the change is logged to this write ahead log first, a simple, sequential, fast append.

Once that log entry is safely written, the write can be acknowledged as durable, even though the actual data page has not necessarily been updated in its final location yet, that update happens shortly after, in the background. If a crash happens before that background update completes, the database replays the write ahead log on restart to recover the change.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032378768-233931838.png
blocks.alt: A write is first logged to the write ahead log, acknowledged as durable, and the actual data page is updated on disk shortly after

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The write ahead log is what lets a database acknowledge a write as durable quickly, without waiting for the slower, final update to the actual data page on disk. Understanding this explains why crash recovery is genuinely reliable.
7. Genuinely Common Misunderstandings

A few real misunderstandings about this architecture show up often. Assuming every query reads directly from disk, missing the genuinely large role the buffer pool plays in real world performance. Assuming a write is durable the instant a query returns, with no understanding of why, missing the actual role the write ahead log plays in making that guarantee real.
And ignoring the planner entirely, writing queries with no real sense of how they will actually execute, missing real opportunities to write queries that the planner can execute efficiently.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032380304-943036316.png
blocks.alt: Common misunderstandings: assuming every read hits disk directly, assuming durability with no understanding of the write ahead log, and ignoring the planner entirely

9. A Quick Reference Query
Most databases let you actually inspect the execution plan a query will use, revealing which layers of this architecture it will actually touch.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 501;

blocks.content: 10. Common Mistakes

["Treating the database as a black box with no internal structure: understanding the real layers explains a great deal about actual performance behavior.","Assuming a restarted database performs identically to one that has been running: a cold buffer pool genuinely means slower initial performance.","Never checking an actual execution plan: the planner output reveals real, actionable detail about how a query will actually run."]
items: Treating the database as a black box with no internal structure: understanding the real layers explains a great deal about actual performance behavior.
Assuming a restarted database performs identically to one that has been running: a cold buffer pool genuinely means slower initial performance.
Never checking an actual execution plan: the planner output reveals real, actionable detail about how a query will actually run.
